Plus or Minus

ParityGame Strategy
Game: Take turns putting + or − between the numbers. When every gap is filled, you win if the total is odd.
How to play: Choose + or −, then press an empty gap. The computer answers in another gap.

Look for the math

You and the computer argue over plus and minus signs, yet for any fixed length N the winner never changes. The secret is parity: odd versus even.

Negating never flips parity

The expression is always 1 ± 2 ± 3 ± … ± N. Replacing a plus in front of k with a minus replaces +k by −k. An even number stays even when you change its sign; an odd number stays odd. So every choice of signs leaves the same odd/even answer as plain addition 1 + 2 + … + N.

The triangular number decides

That sum is the triangular number N(N + 1) / 2. It is odd exactly when N leaves a remainder of 1 or 2 on division by 4 (N ≡ 1 or 2 (mod 4)). The logic test checks every possible signing for every N from 2 to 12: each one matches that parity. For N up to 20 it also checks that filling the last gap always names the winner the triangular number predicts.

The computer’s randomness is a red herring

The applet’s computer picks a random empty gap and a random sign. That looks like a fight, but it cannot change who wins. Try a short sequence first, as the page suggests: for N = 2 you always win; for N = 3 the computer always does.

Turn Random size off, set N to 5 (you should win) and then to 6 (the computer should win), and play both out. The signs you choose never save a lost length.
